usage: any upper-body garment takes 입다, never 신다/쓰다
따갑다 (prickly) is the #1 wool complaint; don't say 가렵다, which is 'my skin itches'
clothing is counted with the counter 벌, not the generic 개
Koreans size up a sweater by thickness, so 얇다·두껍다 are the habitual adjectives
examples: 오늘은 좀 쌀쌀해서 니트 입었어요.
It's a bit chilly today so I wore a knit.
simplest frame: weather reason + 입다 in casual 해요체
이 니트 목 부분이 따가운데 다른 색도 있어요?
The neck of this knit is itchy — do you have other colors too?
real in-store line; 따갑다 describes the prickly wool sensation, not skin itch
캐시미어 니트는 보풀이 잘 생겨서 손빨래해야 해요.
Cashmere knits pill easily so you have to hand-wash them.
care talk: 보풀이 생기다 = to pill, 손빨래 = hand-wash
nuance: 니트 comes from English 'knit', but in everyday Korean it has narrowed to mean one specific thing: a sweater-type pullover top, the fall/winter staple — NOT 'any knitted item' as in English. Its near-synonym 스웨터 exists but sounds slightly dated or textbook-ish; a real Korean shopper says 니트 far more often, and the two are interchangeable when they do appear. The dividing line worth knowing is 니트 (a finished sweater garment) versus 가디건 (an open-front knit you button up): both are knitwear, but 니트 closes over the head while 가디건 opens at the front. Register is fully neutral — you can say 니트 to anyone. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the verb: because you put it on the body you must use 입다, and saying 니트를 신다 (that's for shoes) or 쓰다 (hats/glasses) sounds badly wrong. Also resist the literal logic 'knit = anything knitted'; in Korean it is the garment, and the prickly complaint is 따갑다, distinct from 가렵다 (skin itching).

usage: outerwear still uses 입다, the universal 'wear-on-body' verb
the two lengths Koreans almost always specify by name
warmth is the whole selling point, so 따뜻하다 is the default praise
counted with the clothing counter 벌, not 개
examples: 겨울에 패딩 하나 사려고요.
I'm thinking of buying a padded jacket for winter.
simple intent: -려고요 (planning to), neutral 해요체
올해는 롱패딩보다 숏패딩이 유행이래요.
They say short padding is trendier than long padding this year.
trend talk: 유행이다 = to be in style, -래요 = I heard
이 패딩 거위털이라서 가벼운데도 진짜 따뜻해요.
This one's goose down, so it's light yet really warm.
spec talk: 거위털 = goose down vs 오리털 = duck down vs 솜 = synthetic
nuance: 패딩 is a Konglish clipping of 'padded (jacket)' and names the quilted, down- or fiber-filled puffer that is Korea's winter essential. The key contrast for a learner is 패딩 vs 코트: a 코트 is a wool/dressy overcoat, while 패딩 is the puffy insulated one — calling every winter coat 코트 is the most common slip, because to Koreans they are different categories of garment. You will rarely hear 패딩 used bare; people specify length, 롱패딩 (below the knee, once almost a school uniform among students) or 숏패딩 (hip-length), and the fill (거위털 goose down / 오리털 duck down / 솜 synthetic) which drives both warmth and price. Register is neutral and everyday. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: use 입다 (not 신다/쓰다) since it's body clothing, and don't default to 코트 for a puffer — and remember Koreans treat 'down jacket' as one fixed word 패딩 rather than translating 'down' (오리털/거위털) into the name.

usage: it's a top, so the verb is 입다
걸치다 = casually layer/throw on, looser than 입다
기모 = brushed inner fleece, the key warmth keyword in winter listings
examples: 저는 집에서 후드티 자주 입어요.
I often wear a hoodie at home.
simplest frame: habit + 자주, casual loungewear
쌀쌀할 때 후드티 하나 걸치면 딱이에요.
When it's chilly, throwing on a hoodie is just right.
쌀쌀하다 = chilly; 걸치다 signals casual layering, 딱이다 = perfect fit/just right
겨울엔 안에 기모 들어간 후드티가 훨씬 따뜻해요.
In winter a fleece-lined hoodie is much warmer.
shopping keyword: 기모 들어가다 = to have inner fleece
nuance: 후드티 is a homegrown Korean coinage stitching English 'hood' onto 티 (from 티셔츠, T-shirt) — literally 'hood-tee' — and means a pullover hooded sweatshirt; think of it as a 맨투맨 (crewneck sweatshirt) with a hood added. The sharp near-synonym contrast is 후드티 (pullover, goes over the head) vs 후드집업 (the zip-up hooded jacket, 집업 from 'zip-up'): Koreans name these as two distinct products, so a learner who lumps them together will ask for the wrong rack. Note also that the bare English word 'hoodie' would be transliterated 후디, but the standard, natural Korean is 후드티 — write and say that. Register is casual and youthful but totally acceptable in everyday speech. Pitfalls: use 입다 (or the breezier 걸치다 for 'throw on'), not 신다/쓰다; and don't import the English spelling 후디. usage: all footwear uses 신다, never 입다
shoes are counted with the pair-counter 켤레
맞다 = to fit; size questions hinge on this verb
examples: 겨울에는 부츠를 자주 신어요.
In winter I often wear boots.
simplest frame: season + 신다, reinforcing the footwear verb
이 부츠 245로 신어 봐도 돼요?
Can I try these boots in 245?
in-store request; Korean shoe sizes are in mm (240, 245, 250), -아도 돼요? asks permission
롱부츠는 종아리가 껴서 발목 부츠로 샀어요.
Tall boots felt tight on my calves, so I got ankle boots instead.
fit problem: 종아리가 끼다 = calves feel tight/squeezed
nuance: 부츠 is straightforwardly English 'boots' and covers footwear rising above the ankle. The single most important thing for an English speaker is the verb: shoes and boots take 신다 (put on the feet), and 입다 — the verb for body clothing — is simply wrong here, a mistake learners make constantly because English uses one word 'wear' for everything. Korean also splits the counter: clothing is 벌 but footwear is 켤레 (a pair), so 부츠 한 켤레, never 부츠 한 개. Lengths get named — 발목 부츠 (ankle boots, also 앵클부츠) vs 롱부츠 (tall boots) — and winter shearling ones are 털부츠 (털 = fur). One more practical trap: Korean shoe sizes are millimeters (245 means 245 mm), so quote the number, not a US/EU size. Register is neutral; say 부츠 to anyone.

usage: 기본 = staple, no graphic print — a common search filter
어울리다 = to look good on / go well with
examples: 저는 맨투맨을 제일 자주 입어요.
I wear sweatshirts the most.

후드티 말고 맨투맨으로 보여 주세요.

맨투맨에 청바지 하나면 무난하게 입기 좋아요.

The decisive near-synonym contrast is 맨투맨 (no hood) vs 후드티 (hood added): they are the same body of garment differing only by the hood, and Koreans pick the word precisely, so mixing them up sends you to the wrong product. usage: a top layer worn on the body, so 입다
걸치다 fits open-front layers you don't fully button
the office air-con staple; 얇다 = thin
examples: 봄에는 얇은 가디건 하나면 충분해요.
In spring one thin cardigan is enough.
simplest frame: season + 하나면 충분하다 (one is enough)
원피스 위에 가디건 하나 걸치면 예뻐요.
Draping a cardigan over a dress looks nice.
걸치다 (layer loosely) suits the open front; 위에 = on top of
사무실 에어컨이 세서 가디건을 챙겨 다녀요.
The office AC is strong so I carry a cardigan around.
real office life: 챙기다 = to bring along, 에어컨이 세다 = AC is strong
nuance: 가디건 is the open-front knit layer you close with buttons or a zip — English 'cardigan'. There is a spelling fork worth flagging: the prescriptive standard is 카디건, but in real life and in online shops almost everyone writes and says 가디건, so that's the form you'll actually encounter. Register is neutral. Pitfalls: don't insist on 카디건 in conversation when you mean to be understood and find it in a search bar — say 가디건; and use 입다/걸치다, not 신다/쓰다. usage: 비치다 = to show through; the make-or-break concern when buying
the activewear context that pairs with 요가/운동
clothing counter 벌 — NOT 켤레, which is for shoes
examples: 저는 운동할 때 레깅스를 입어요.
I wear leggings when I work out.
simplest frame: activity + 입다, anchoring the activewear use
이 레깅스 앉으면 비치지 않아요?
Don't these leggings show through when you sit down?
the universal fitting-room question; 비치다 = to be see-through
요즘은 레깅스만 입고 카페 가는 사람도 많아요.
These days lots of people go to cafés in just leggings.

usage: 삼선 = 'three stripes', the famous casual-student style nickname
실내용 (Sino-Korean 室內用) = for indoor use
examples: 집에서는 항상 슬리퍼를 신어요.
At home I always wear slippers.
simplest frame: place + 신다, reinforcing footwear verb
편의점 갈 때는 그냥 슬리퍼 신고 나가요.

사무실에 신을 슬리퍼 하나 사 두면 편해요.

The crucial near-synonym line is 슬리퍼 vs 쪼리: the thong type with a strap between the toes is its own word 쪼리 (flip-flops), so calling those 슬리퍼 is imprecise — slides are 슬리퍼, thongs are 쪼리. usage: the popular sleeveless puffer for in-between weather
even just a vest keeps you warm
examples: 오늘은 조끼만 입어도 충분해요.
Just a vest is enough today.
simplest frame: -만 ...도 (even only ~), neutral 해요체
니트 위에 조끼 하나 입으면 따뜻해요.
A vest over a knit keeps you warm.
layering: 위에 = on top of, the standard way to stack pieces
애매하게 추울 때 패딩 조끼가 딱이에요.
When it's awkwardly chilly, a puffer vest is perfect.
애매하게 춥다 = 'not-quite-cold', a very natural in-between-season phrase
nuance: 조끼 is a native Korean word (not a loanword) for a sleeveless top layer — it covers the torso while leaving the arms free. The near-synonym to know is the loanword 베스트 (from English 'vest'), which tends to be used for the dressy waistcoat in a suit, whereas plain 조끼 is the all-purpose everyday/outdoor sleeveless layer; both can mean 'vest', but a Korean reaches for 조끼 for the casual or padded kind. The hugely popular variant is 패딩 조끼 (puffer vest), a go-to for 환절기/간절기 (the changing seasons), and the arm-freedom makes 조끼 a favorite for hiking and outdoor work. The main contrast students confuse is 조끼 (sleeveless) vs 가디건 (sleeved open-front knit) — if it has sleeves it isn't a 조끼. Register is neutral. Use 입다, not 신다/쓰다; it's body clothing despite covering only the trunk.

usage: neck accessories commonly take the light verb 하다
두르다 = to wrap/drape around, very natural for neck/shoulders
the typical material; silk ones are popular gifts
a thin flat cloth is counted with 장 (the sheet-counter)
examples: 오늘은 스카프를 했어요.
I wore a scarf today.
simplest frame showing the accessory verb 하다, not 입다
목에 스카프 하나 두르면 분위기가 확 달라져요.
Wrapping a scarf around your neck totally changes the vibe.
fashion talk: 두르다 = to wrap, 분위기 = mood/vibe, 확 = dramatically
선물용으로 실크 스카프 하나 샀어요.
I bought a silk scarf as a gift.
선물용 = for gifting; flat cloth, so counted 한 장
nuance: 스카프 (English 'scarf') in Korean specifically means the LIGHT, decorative cloth — often silk — you tie around the neck, head, or even a bag handle, worn for style rather than warmth. The essential near-synonym contrast is 스카프 vs 목도리/머플러: 목도리 (native word) and 머플러 (from 'muffler') are the thick, warm winter neck-wraps, while 스카프 is the thin fashion piece — confusing them means wearing the wrong thing for the wrong purpose. The verb is its own pitfall: accessories like this take 하다 ('스카프를 하다') or 두르다 ('wrap'), and the body-clothing verb 입다 is wrong here, just as it would be for 모자 (which takes 쓰다). Because it's a thin flat sheet, the counter is 장, not the clothing counter 벌. Register is neutral. A current collocation: tying a 스카프 onto a 가방 (bag) is a popular styling trick.

usage: to carry a backpack (on the back/shoulder)
shoulder- and back-worn bags use 메다, not 들다
bags are counted with the generic counter 개
the commuter/student staple; 노트북 수납 = laptop storage is a top spec
weight is a leading buying factor, so 가볍다 recurs in reviews
examples: 저는 보통 백팩을 메고 다녀요.
I usually carry a backpack around.
simplest frame: habit + 메다, anchoring the bag verb
출퇴근할 때 노트북 넣을 백팩이 필요해요.
I need a backpack to put my laptop in for commuting.
real need: 출퇴근 = commute, 넣을 = relative form 'to put in'
이 백팩은 수납공간이 많아서 마음에 들어요.
I like this backpack because it has lots of storage.
feature praise: 수납공간 = storage compartments, 마음에 들다 = to like
nuance: 백팩 is English 'backpack' and names the two-shoulder bag carried on the back. The verb is the heart of the matter: bags worn on the shoulder or back take 메다, while 들다 means to carry by hand (a tote, a paper bag) and is wrong for a backpack — English's single 'carry' hides this, so 백팩을 들다 is a classic slip when you mean wearing it on your back. The useful near-synonym contrast is 백팩 vs 배낭 (Sino-Korean 背囊, literally 'back-bag'): 배낭 carries a strong hiking/trekking, outdoorsy flavor (think 배낭여행 = backpacking trip), whereas 백팩 is the everyday, commuter, fashion-bag word — they overlap but feel different, so reaching for 배낭 to describe a sleek office bag sounds slightly off. usage: 갈아입다 = to change (one outfit) into (another); -으로 marks the result
벌 here counts a top-and-bottom set, not a single piece
examples: 운동할 때는 운동복을 입어요.
I wear workout clothes when I exercise.
simplest frame: activity + 입다, neutral 해요체
헬스장 가기 전에 운동복으로 갈아입어요.
Before the gym I change into workout clothes.
routine: 헬스장 = gym, 갈아입다 = change into, -기 전에 = before ~ing
땀 잘 마르는 운동복으로 하나 사려고요.
I'm planning to buy activewear that dries sweat fast.
real spec: 땀이 마르다 = sweat dries; -려고요 = planning to
nuance: 운동복 is a transparent Sino-Korean + native compound: 운동 (運動, 'exercise/movement') + 복 (服, 'clothing') = literally 'exercise-clothes', the umbrella term for activewear, both top and bottom. Because the hanja 복 means 'clothing/garment' generally, you'll meet it across many words (교복 school uniform, 한복 traditional dress, 수영복 swimsuit), which makes 운동복 easy to decode once you know the building block. The near-synonym to weigh is 트레이닝복 (from 'training'): that leans toward the matching tracksuit/sweats set (casually 츄리닝), while 운동복 spans gym, yoga, and running gear more broadly — overlapping but not identical. A subtle point for English speakers: 운동복 normally denotes a top-and-bottom SET, so it's counted 한 벌 and 'wear' is 입다, not 신다/쓰다. With athleisure now everywhere, people 평소에도 (even normally) wear 운동복, so it surfaces well beyond the gym. Register is neutral.
